summary.text:
A council leaning short into a curve MUFG expects to fall. At 31 March 2025 only 15% of debt matured inside 12 months; the same paper's TMSS forecasts 29% at 1 April 2026, and lifts the 1–5 year upper limit from 60% to 65% to accommodate more of the same. All £30m of 2024/25 new borrowing was 15–18 month PWLB. The paper says why: matching capital-receipt timing on GF projects, plus an HRA HSF profile that has already moved shorter.

The single amber prudential indicator flagged by Audit and Governance for Council's comment was the GF financing cost ratio at 25.8% for 2024/25 against a 24.3% plan. Read on its own it looks like a 1.5pp overshoot. Read against the 2026/27 TMSS forecasts for the same ratio — 25.3%, 26.8%, 27.4%, 27.5% to 2028/29 — it is the start of a permanent step-up, not a one-year miss.

An unusually specific disclosure: HRA HSF refinancing 'will be necessary' in 2026/27, and the paper attributes it verbatim to 'reduced income due to changes in Government rent policy and 2 years when rent increases agreed by the Council were lower than those recommended by Cabinet in 2012/13 and 2013/14'. Not many councils name two historic rent decisions as the direct cause of a current refinancing lump.

officer.subject: The amber indicator, and what the 26/27 TMSS says happens next
officer.body:
Hi Linda,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are some thoughts from your Annual Treasury Management Report that went to Council on 25 February, offered as background before whatever the next treasury report to Audit and Governance turns out to be. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. It's a clear, honest report and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

A note on scope up front: our file holds the PWLB book, not LOBOs or market debt, and for St Albans the historic HSF long-dated loans sit under tranche dates in our data that don't line up with a 31 March 2025 filter, so we can't reproduce your £202.8m from Appendix 1 the way we'd normally open with. Everything below is drawn from your own paper rather than from a reconciliation.

The amber indicator was the one item Audit and Governance asked Council to comment on — GF financing costs to net revenue at 25.8% for 2024/25 against a 24.3% plan. Read alone it looks like a 1.5% overshoot. The 2026/27 TMSS tabled the same day sets that ratio at 25.3%, 26.8%, 27.4% and 27.5% for the next four years, and the HRA ratio at 54.5%, 47.2%, 50.6% and 43.4%. So the amber print isn't a one-year miss, it's the start of a permanent step-up. Members may not have that context to hand when the outturn ratio and the strategy ratios sit in two different papers.

The other thing worth flagging is the maturity shift. At 31 March 2025 only 15% of debt matured inside twelve months. Appendix 14 Table 12 estimates 29% at 1 April 2026, and lifts the 1–5 year upper limit from 60% to 65% to make room for more of it. All £30m of 2024/25 new borrowing was 15–18 month PWLB, and the 2026/27 strategy pipelines a further £192m of gross borrowing over the four years to 2028/29 on top of your £203m existing stock. The paper explains why — matching new loans to capital-receipt timing on GF projects, and an HSF profile that has already moved shorter — and MUFG's 22 December 2025 forecast (Table 11) had Bank Rate falling to 3.25% and the 5-year PWLB certainty rate to 4.10% by early 2027, which supports leaning short. Where the market has actually gone since is close to what MUFG projected: Friday's certainty curve (notice 314/26 PM) has 5yr at 4.38%, 10yr at 4.87%, 25yr at 5.54% and 50yr at 5.34%, so the short-end forecast is close to already delivered.

One more thing that stood out. Appendix 14 attributes the 2026/27 HSF refinancing lump verbatim to 'changes in Government rent policy and 2 years when rent increases agreed by the Council were lower than those recommended by Cabinet in 2012/13 and 2013/14'. Not many treasury reports name two historic rent decisions as the direct cause of a current refinancing requirement — most either don't say why or blame the general environment. It's a useful disclosure and the sort of thing a member scrutinising the strategy would want to see kept.

The monthly sector page at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity is where you can watch how the £192m pipeline is landing relative to what other councils are drawing at each tenor — July was £368m across 33 loans at an average 5.02% after the thinnest May in years, so the market is choppy. And the rates page at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard takes ten seconds to check before you fix.

None of this needs a meeting or a subscription. On training, four look most relevant to St Albans given what the strategy is doing: Interest rate risk, for the 29% short-end tilt; Strategic PWLB borrowing, for the £192m pipeline; HRA treasury, for the HSF refinancing sequence and the 28 January PWLB discount extension you already reference; and our liability benchmark pathway, which is interactive and built on live data — worth a look given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Codes. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
